L	“Last night she came to me again.”
In the dream, they were girls once more, sitting on opposite beds, their legs not touching the
marble floor. Damla’s braid fell thick against her shoulder. “We hadn’t aged at all,” the narrator
recalls. But this time Damla had returned “to tell me something.” That summer had begun
without ceremony. “We'll take her,” the father had said in the dark house in the hills. “The girls
will sleep in one room. They’re basically sisters.” Damla did not look up. There was bitter tea,
wrapped sweets, and a silence that felt heavier than words. The village lay open toward the sea—
“like the world opening up.” Boats rolled down the sand in bright colors, and the two girls took
refuge in the cabin of Penelope. Captain would find them crouched inside cabinets. “Girls, girls,
girls,” he laughed once. “What're you doing here again, with all the ghosts?” “Do you think it’s
true?” Damla asked afterward. “We'll wait here and see if they come,” she said. They summoned
names they barely understood. “Melike,” Damla whispered into a shell pressed to the floor of the
rocking cabin. “We want to talk to you.” The shell slid across the wood. Pebbles swished outside.
At night, beneath a ceiling fan and mosquito net, they lay on their backs. “She died, but she didn’t
leave,” the narrator said of Melike. “Did you ever see her afterward?” Damla asked. “No.” They
were fearless together. “We owned the world with our stories.” They imagined ropes loosening,
sails speaking, the sea answering back. They did not imagine consequence. One afternoon they
saw Uncle laughing with Captain. Damla shrank. “Are they friends, then?” she asked quietly. The
narrator shrugged. “Does he ever ask about me?” Damla pressed. “Yes,” she said. “Sometimes.” It
might not have been true. The next day they untied the “sturdiest knots,” impatient for something
to happen—for the ghost to come. Nothing was said when Captain climbed the mast. They
watched from below. “We might have stepped forward to warn him about the ropes,” the narrator
admits. They were forming the words. Waiting. There was a moment—just before he fell—“that he
floated in the air.” Years later, the narrator hears that there is a poster of Damla in the
coffeehouse. She has not returned to the village. She remembers only the summer when they
believed themselves “irrelevant as ghosts,” and wonders what they truly disturbed.

questions.stimulus:
I.	Few puzzles expose the limits of human intuition as sharply as the Monty Hall Problem. The
scenario is deceptively simple: three doors, one car, two goats. You select a door. The host—who
knows where the car is—opens another door, deliberately revealing a goat. You are then offered a
choice: stay with your original selection or switch.
Most people instinctively reason that once a goat has been revealed, only two doors remain, and
therefore the odds must be evenly split. The situation appears symmetrical. Two unopened doors.
One prize. A 50/50 gamble.
But symmetry here is an illusion.
Your initial choice had only a one-in-three chance of being correct. The remaining two doors
collectively held a two-in-three probability of hiding the car. When the host opens a goat door—
crucially, one he knows to be empty—he is not redistributing probability. He is revealing
information. The entire two-in-three likelihood collapses onto the single unopened alternative.
Staying preserves your original one-in-three odds. Switching transfers you to the two-in-three
probability you initially rejected.
For those who find this explanation unconvincing, expanding the problem clarifies the logic.
Imagine 100 doors instead of three. You choose one. The host opens 98 others, each containing
goats. Two doors remain: yours and one other. It now feels far less plausible that your original
pick—made when the odds were one in one hundred—should suddenly become equally likely.
Yet resistance to this reasoning is remarkably common. When the correct solution was published
in a widely read column in 1990, thousands of readers insisted it was wrong. Even mathematically
trained individuals struggled to accept it. The discomfort reveals something important: human
reasoning is deeply shaped by surface appearance rather than probabilistic structure.
The Monty Hall Problem is not merely about doors and goats. It is about how easily intuition can
mislead us—and how reluctantly we surrender it, even when confronted with proof.
Source: Adapted from a widely discussed probability puzzle known as The Monty Hall Problem,
originally popularized in 1990 through Marilyn vos Savant’s Ask Marilyn column in Parade
magazine.

Il.	Franz Kafka is buried in Prague’s New Jewish Cemetery, where visitors leave candles, pens, and
painted stones beside his headstone. Given that Kafka instructed his friend Max Brod to burn his
manuscripts “unread,” one suspects he would not have welcomed the crowds. Whenever I visit his
grave or pass the numerous cafés, bookstores, museums, and souvenir shops bearing his name, I
find myself thinking: He would hate this. www.lawpreptutorial.com

Kafka Bookstore, Kafka restaurants, exhibitions, hostels, and even high-end merchandise carrying
his signature. His image has been monumentalized, commodified, and mythologized. The “Kafka
Industry” does not operate only at the level of tourism; it thrives equally in high culture.
Biographies, adaptations, films, academic conferences, and critical studies have multiplied to the
point where the words written about Kafka vastly exceed those written by him.
This construction of Kafka began early. Max Brod, who preserved and published his friend’s
manuscripts, also fashioned an image of Kafka as a saintly seer—an allegorical prophet whose
works were to be decoded across generations. Later commentators extended this portrait. What
emerged was not merely Kafka the writer, but Kafka the symbol. Milan Kundera later criticized
what he called “Kafkology,” arguing that critics often replaced Kafka with a “Kafkologized Kafka,”
an image so heavily interpreted that it obscured the author himself.

Yet Kafka’s historical context complicates matters. He lived as a German-speaking Jew in Prague
at a time of rising nationalism and anti-Semitism. His city was transforming; the old Jewish
quarter was demolished, and violence periodically erupted. Under Communist rule his works were
banned for “decadent anti-realism,” only to be reclaimed during the Prague Spring. Each political
regime seemed to discover its own Kafka.

Agnieszka Holland’s film Franz presents a restrained portrait of Kafka as a private man rather
than a prophet. Yet the very act of producing another film contributes to what it seeks to resist.
Any effort to present “the real Kafka” inevitably adds another layer to the growing edifice of
interpretation.

no image of Gregor’s transformed body appear on the cover. He resisted easy visualization and
feared that interpretation would smother the work. But denial invites curiosity. The result is a
paradox: it feels impossible to write anything new about Kafka, and yet impossible not to write
about him.

commercialize, and canonize. The industry continues to grow—even this essay becomes part of it.

(December 2025)

IV.	They tell her she can be rewritten. They say she can be pressed into the margins of history,
distorted by “twisted lies,” ” dragged through dust, stamped into the ground until nothing
recognizable remains. She hears them. She does not pretend the voices are absent. But like dust—
restless, inevitable, rising at the slightest disturbance—she rises.
Their objections turn personal. Why is she so confident? Why does she laugh as though she owns
the room? Why does her presence feel like possession? She smiles at the accusation and answers
without apology: “Because I do.” Not with gold, not with property, but with dignity stored deep in
the marrow. She walks as though abundance runs beneath her feet, as though worth is not
granted but inherent.
They warn her she will not survive. They threaten silence. They promise words sharp enough to
cut bone. The intention is clear: diminish, contain, erase. Yet the answer remains unchanged.
Still—she rises.
Her rising does not begin with her. It stands on backs bent under chains, on hands hardened by
labor, on grief swallowed so children might eat. “I carried bricks until my back broke,” one voice
says. “I swallowed grief,” another echoes. The weight of history presses forward, but she refuses to
crouch beneath it. She acknowledges where she comes from. She will not kneel there.
They command her to shrink. To stay in her place. To bend. But her ascent moves like the moon
drawing tides, like the sun insisting on morning. It obeys a law older than cruelty. When they
demand to know why she does not break, she answers simply: resilience is elemental. It is not
borrowed. It is born.
The “I” she speaks is no longer solitary. It gathers mothers, daughters, unnamed spirits—those
told they were too dark, too loud, too much; those told they were nothing at all. The rising becomes
plural. It becomes shared. It becomes luminous.
She does not request permission. She does not bargain for worth. She names herself “the dream
and the hope of those who endured the unendurable.” And when the final question comes—“And
you?”—she answers without hesitation.
“T rise.”
And still—she rises.
Source: Inspired by “Still I Rise” — Maya Angelou

VII. Manipur has been facing prolonged ethnic violence since (1), primarily between the Meitei
community, largely residing in the Imphal Valley, and the Kuki-Zo tribal groups inhabiting the
hill districts. What began as tensions over identity and constitutional protections escalated into
one of the most severe internal security crises in the state’s recent history.
The immediate trigger for the violence was a solidarity march organised by tribal groups to protest
the Manipur government’s alleged move to grant Scheduled Tribe (ST) status to the Meitei
community. The Kuki-Zo groups opposed this proposal, fearing it would dilute existing affirmative
action benefits, affect land ownership rights in the hills, and weaken their political representation.
These long-standing issues relating to land, reservations, and power-sharing deepened mistrust
and led to widespread unrest.
The violence rapidly spread across the state, resulting in more than 250 deaths and the
displacement of nearly 60,000 people. Many displaced individuals continue to reside in relief
camps. The crisis was marked by repeated curfews, extended internet shutdowns, and persistent
instability, which effectively segregated communities and disrupted normal life across large parts
of Manipur.
As the unrest continued, then Chief Minister N. Biren Singh came under increasing criticism for
his inability to restore peace. Political instability intensified, and on February 9, 2025, after nearly
20 months of violence and amid the threat of a no-confidence motion in the Manipur Legislative
Assembly, he resigned Following this, President’s Rule was imposed, indicating a breakdown of
constitutional governance in the state.
Manipur’s (2) Legislative Assembly, elected in 2022 with a term running until 2027, has 37 BJP
MLAs, including seven from the Kuki-Zo community. In early 2026, efforts to restore an elected
government gained momentum. On February 2, 2026, the BJP appointed Tarun Chugh as central
observer to oversee the election of its Legislature Party leader. The next day, Yumnam
Khemchand Singh was elected leader, paving the way for his appointment as Chief Minister.
Reports also suggest that Nemcha Kipgen, a Kuki-Zo MLA, is likely to be appointed Deputy Chief
Minister, signalling an attempt at political reconciliation and inclusive governance.

IX.	The Indian National Congress, founded in 1885, initially emerged as a platform for dialogue
between educated Indian elites and the British colonial administration. In its early phase, the
Congress relied on constitutional methods such as petitions, resolutions, and appeals, reflecting
the belief that political progress could be achieved through gradual reforms within the colonial
framework. This approach was shaped by the socio-political context of the time, where mass
political mobilization was neither feasible nor widely accepted
However, the limitations of this moderate strategy became increasingly evident in the early
twentieth century. The failure of the British government to respond meaningfully to Indian
demands, combined with economic hardships and racial discrimination, led to growing
disillusionment among nationalist leaders. As a result, the Congress gradually transformed its

methods and objectives, incorporating mass participation and more assertive forms of protest. This
shift marked a significant change in the nature of the nationalist movement—from elite
negotiation to popular mobilization.
The entry of Mahatma Gandhi into the Congress further altered its character. By emphasizing
non-violence and mass participation, Gandhi enabled the Congress to reach peasants, workers, and
marginalized groups, thereby broadening its social base. Movements such as Non-Cooperation and
Civil Disobedience reflected this new strategy, which sought to challenge colonial authority by
undermining its moral and administrative legitimacy rather than relying solely on constitutional
agitation.
Despite internal disagreements and periodic setbacks, the Congress remained the central force of
the Indian freedom struggle. Its ability to adapt to changing political circumstances, balance
ideological differences, and integrate diverse social interests allowed it to sustain relevance over
decades. The evolution of the Indian National Congress thus illustrates how nationalist
movements often reshape their strategies in response to political realities, rather than following a
fixed ideological path.
Source: Themes in Indian History — Part II “Colonialism and the Countryside / The Nationalist
Movement”)

achieving the goal of a developed India by (1). The Finance Minister highlighted investments in

pattern over the past decade. The share of revenue expenditure in total expenditure has declined
significantly from 88% in 2014-15 to about 77% in 2026-27 (BE), a reduction of 11 percentage
points. A major contributor to this decline has been a reduction in central subsidies, which fell by
about 7 percentage points. Correspondingly, the share of capital expenditure has increased,
reflecting the government’s intent to promote growth through infrastructure and asset creation.

COVID period, when it remained high as a percentage of GDP. However, its growth rate has
steadily declined—from 28.3% in 2023-24 to 10.8% in 2024-25 and further to 4.2% in 2025-26
(RE). Although capital expenditure is budgeted to grow by 11.5% in 2026-27, this is only
marginally higher than the projected nominal GDP growth of 10%, implying that capital
expenditure will remain almost stagnant at around 3.1% of GDP.

buoyancy of gross tax revenues has fallen to 0.8, below the desirable benchmark of 1. While direct

SECTION III
XII. The Supreme Court has overturned the Allahabad high court’s observation that assaulting a
minor by grabbing her breasts and attempting to disrobe her did not amount to attempted rape,
and has directed the formation of a panel to draft sensitivity guidelines for judges handling sexual
offence cases.
On February 10, 2026 the Supreme Court set aside the Allahabad High Court's March 17, 2025
order that had controversially held that the acts of grabbing a child’s breasts, breaking her pyjama
string, and attempting to drag her under a culvert did not amount to rape or attempted rape.
A bench of CJI Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and NV Anjaria ruled that such acts
clearly constituted attempted rape/penetrative sexual assault under the POCSO Act, rejecting the
high court's view that they were merely “preparatory.”
"We cannot agree with the finding of the high court that the allegations only amount to
preparation, but not an attempt, towards the commission of the offence of rape,” the SC bench
ruled.
Further, the bench emphasised that adjudication in sexual offence cases must be rooted in law and
empathy, cautioning that justice cannot be delivered if courts are “inconsiderate” to victims’
vulnerabilities.
In its judgment delivered on February 10, the bench cautioned that courts cannot deliver
“complete justice” if they are “inconsiderate” to the vulnerabilities of litigants.
"The court's decisions must reflect the ethos of compassion, humanity, and understanding, which
are essential for creating a fair and effective justice system,’ the bench said.
It stressed the need for systemic correction and greater sensitivity among judges, noting that
judicial decisions must reflect compassion, humanity, and understanding. Training and guidelines
are required to nurture sensitivity in handling sexual offence cases.
The Allahabad High Court had made the controversial observations on March 17, 2025, while
modifying a summoning order against two accused persons. According to the prosecution, the
accused, Pawan and Akash, allegedly assaulted an 11-year-old girl, grabbing her breasts, breaking
her pyjama string, and trying to drag her beneath a culvert. However, they fled after passers-by
intervened.
The trial court charged them under Section 376 IPC (rape) and Section 18 POCSO (attempt). The
high court, however, reduced charges to Section 354-B IPC (assault with intent to disrobe) and
Sections 9/10 POCSO (aggravated sexual assault), stating there was no “determined intent” to
commit rape.
The SC later took suo motu cognizance of the order and stayed it on March 26, 2025. However, it
declined to frame any immediate guidelines itself, citing the need for a comprehensive study.
The SC has now directed the National Judicial Academy (NJA), Bhopal to form a committee of
experts to draft guidelines to inculcate "sensitivity and compassion" in judges and judicial
processes in cases of sexual offences.
The SC also stressed that the guidelines must be in simple, accessible language, avoiding complex
foreign expressions, and asked the NJA to submit its report preferably within three months.
Source: https://thefederal.com/category /news/sc-overturns-allahabad-hc-controversial-order-
child-assault-case-judicial-empathy-230406

and is authorized to do so. For example, if an agent of a real estate company commits fraud while
representing the company in a transaction, the company may be held liable for the agent’s actions.

generally considered to be operating as a separate business entity.

XIV. The Supreme Court of India recently expressed grave concern over an emerging and what it
termed an "alarming" trend of lawyers using artificial intelligence tools to draft court petitions
often without adequate verification. A bench comprising Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and
Justices B.V. Nagarathna and Joymalya Bagchi made these pointed remarks while hearing a
Public Interest Litigation (PIL) filed by academician Roop Rekha Verma, which sought the
framing of guidelines governing political speeches. Although the PIL itself pertained to a different
subject matter, the bench seized the opportunity to address a pressing concern that had been
surfacing repeatedly in court filings.
"We are alarmed to reflect that some lawyers have started using AI to draft petitions. It is
absolutely uncalled for," the Chief Justice observed, reflecting the judiciary's deepening unease.
Justice Nagarathna recalled encountering a fictitious citation, a case titled "Mercy vs Mankind"
that simply does not exist in any official law report or judicial record. The Chief Justice further
noted that a similar pattern had emerged before Justice Dipankar Datta, where not one but a
series of fabricated judgments had been cited in support of legal arguments, all of which were
found to be entirely non-existent.
The court also flagged a subtler but equally concerning problem: that even where cited judgments
were genuine, petitions sometimes contained fake quotations attributed to those verdicts. This

forces judges to spend additional time verifying the accuracy of each citation creating, as Justice
Nagarathna put it, "an additional burden on the part of the judges." Justice Bagchi added to these
concerns by lamenting the visible decline in the quality of legal drafting, particularly in special
leave petitions (SLPs). He observed that many such petitions are overloaded with lengthy extracts
from previous judgments, leaving little room for original legal reasoning or structured
argumentation a hallmark of skilled advocacy.
The Supreme Court clarified that it does not oppose the use of technology in legal practice
altogether. Indeed, the Court itself has embraced AI for translating judgments into Indian
languages and for case management through machine learning tools. However, it drew a firm line:
technology may assist with research, but it cannot replace the professional responsibility of an
advocate. Every citation, quotation, and legal proposition, the bench stressed, must be verified
against authentic, authorised sources before being placed on record. A lawyer, as an officer of the
court, carries a duty of diligence that no automated tool can discharge on their behalf. Blind
reliance on Al-generated content, the Court indicated, not only misleads the judiciary but strikes
at the very integrity of legal proceedings.

drafting-petitions/article70644488.ece

questions.stimulus:
XV. The Supreme Court of India, on January 16, 2026, strongly criticised the growing and increasingly
common tendency among litigants to directly invoke Article 32 of the Constitution even in cases
where proceedings on the very same issue are already pending before a High Court. A bench
comprising Justice B.V. Nagarathna and Justice Ujjal Bhuyan took serious note of this practice
while hearing a writ petition filed under Article 32, despite the fact that an identical or
substantially similar plea was already under active consideration before the Bombay High Court.
The bench termed the petition a "gross misuse of the process of the court and of law" and
dismissed it without entertaining it on merits.www.lawpreptutorial.com
Expressing its displeasure in pointed terms, the bench observed that Article 32 was being invoked
with alarming frequency and for increasingly trivial reasons. The Court noted that litigants were
approaching the Supreme Court at even the slightest pretext — including the mere grant of an
adjournment in a High Court — rather than allowing those proceedings to reach their natural
conclusion. "Article 32 is being misused. The number of cases filed under Article 32 is
exponentially increasing. For everything, one adjournment, file Article 32 here. Especially those
surrounding Delhi are filing Article 82 petitions. What is this? It is a misuse," the bench
remarked, reflecting both frustration and constitutional concern.
Article 32 of the Constitution, which confers upon every citizen the fundamental right to approach
the Supreme Court directly for the enforcement of their fundamental rights, is regarded as one of
the most important and cherished provisions in the constitutional framework. Dr. B.R. Ambedkar
had famously described it as the "heart and soul of the Constitution." However, the apex court has
consistently held that this extraordinary remedy is not meant to be treated as a routine or first
resort. It is intended to be invoked only when there is a clear and demonstrated violation of
fundamental rights that warrants the direct intervention of the Supreme Court, and not as a
shortcut to bypass High Courts that are already seized of the same matter.
The Court reiterated that the appropriate constitutional remedy available before High Courts
under Article 226 — which confers a wide and expansive writ jurisdiction — must be exhausted or
at least genuinely engaged with, before a litigant seeks to invoke the Supreme Court's jurisdiction
under Article 32. By dismissing the petition, the bench sent a firm and unambiguous signal
against forum shopping and the casual erosion of the judicial hierarchy that such practices
inevitably bring about.
Source: https://lawtrend.in/supreme-court-slams-misuse-of-article-32-petitions-dismisses-plea-
filed-despite-pending-high-court-case/

In light of the Supreme Court’s observations regarding the misuse of Article 32, consider the
following statements:
1. Article 32 forms part of the Basic Structure of the Constitution.
2. The Supreme Court is constitutionally bound to entertain every petition filed under Article 32
if a Fundamental Right violation is alleged.
3. High Courts under Article 226 have wider writ jurisdiction than the Supreme Court under
Article 32.
4. The power to issue writs under Article 32 can be suspended during a National Emergency
through a Presidential Order under Article 359.
Which of the following options correctly identifies the statements that are legally accurate?

questions.stimulus:
XVI. “Deprivation (total loss) of personal liberty, which inter alia includes the right to eat or sleep when
one likes or to work or not to work as and when one pleases and several such rights sought to be
protected by the expression ‘personal liberty' in Article 21, is quite different from restriction
(which is only a partial control) of the right to move freely (which is relatively a minor right of a
citizen) as safeguarded by Article 19(1)(d). Deprivation of personal liberty has not the same
meaning as restriction of free movement in the territory of India. This is made clear when the
provisions of the Criminal Procedure Code in Chapter VIII relating to security of peace or
maintenance of public order are read. Therefore Article 19(5) cannot apply to a substantive law
depriving a citizen of personal liberty. I am unable to accept the contention that the word
‘deprivation’ includes within its scope 'restriction' when interpreting Article 21. Article 22
envisages the law of preventive detention. So does Article 246 read with Schedule Seven, List I,
Entry 9, and List III, Entry 3. Therefore, when the subject of preventive detention is specifically
dealt with in the Chapter on Fundamental Rights, I do not think it is proper to consider a
legislation permitting preventive detention as in conflict with the rights mentioned in Article
19(1). Article 19(1) does not purport to cover all aspects of liberty or of personal liberty. In that
article only certain phases of liberty are dealt with. www.lawpreptutorial.com
‘Personal liberty' would primarily mean liberty of the physical body. The rights given under Article
19(1) do not directly come under that description. They are rights which accompany the freedom or
liberty of the person. By their very nature they are freedoms of a person assumed to be in full
possession of his personal liberty. If Article 19 is considered to be the only article safeguarding
personal liberty, several well-recognised rights, as for instance, the right to eat or drink, the right
to work, play, swim and numerous other rights and activities and even the right to life will not be
deemed protected under the Constitution. I do not think that is the intention. It seems to me
improper to read Article 19 as dealing with the same subject as Article 21. Article 19 gives the
rights specified therein only to the citizens of India while Article 21 is applicable to all persons.
The word citizen is expressly defined in the Constitution to indicate only a certain section of the
inhabitants of India. Moreover, the protection given by Article 21 is very general. It is of '‘law'-
whatever that expression is interpreted to mean. The legislative restrictions on the law-making
powers of the legislature are not here prescribed in detail as in the case of the rights specified in
Article 19. In my opinion therefore Article 19 should be read as a separate complete article.”
Source: Kania CJ in AK Gopalan v. State of Madras 1950 AIR 27, 1950 SCR 88
